This is the first post in a new blog in which I plan to infrequently post
performance analyses related to [`gitoxide`][gitoxide]. This post is largely a
port of existing code I used in two previous blog posts ([one measuring the
difference between using `imara-diff` 0.1 and 0.2][imara-diff-0-1-vs-0-2],
[another one measuring the effects of optimizing tree diffing by skipping
identical subtrees][skip-identical-subtree-diff]), and it mainly exists to
exercise the new publishing pipeline. The reason I’m now starting this separate
blog is that my main blog runs on Jekyll which is not as well suited to the
kinds of analyses that I want to work on from time to time as Quarto which is
the software behind this new blog.

[gitoxide]: https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide.git
[imara-diff-0-1-vs-0-2]: https://c.rubler.net/blog/2026/01/25/gix-blame-performance-with-imara-diff-0-1-and-0-2.html
[skip-identical-subtree-diff]: https://c.rubler.net/blog/2026/03/14/gix-blame-performance-improved-by-a-change-in-gix-diff.html

In this post, I’m going to compare `gix blame` at commit [`e63d487fb` (from
February 16, 2026)][commit-e63d487fb] with `gix blame` at commit [`9949e9fdf`
(from July 19, 2026)][commit-9949e9fdf] (the latter chosen because it happened
to be `HEAD` when I started writing this post). Specifically, I’m going to
compare the performance of `gix blame` on the same set of 9 files that I used
for the benchmarks of my earlier posts.

[commit-e63d487fb]: https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/commit/e63d487fb1b1425a9458fc7400517ad2c0280fd2
[commit-9949e9fdf]: https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/commit/9949e9fdfa27a6630a8a12f7da07cbdd5c03aeed

## Running the benchmark

After compiling both executables with `cargo build --release --locked`, I ran
the following script to collect some data using `hyperfine`.

```bash
env GIT_DIR="$HOME/github/Byron/gitoxide/.git" BASELINE_EXECUTABLE="$HOME/bin/gix-2026-07-20-e63d487fb" COMPARISON_EXECUTABLE="$HOME/bin/gix-2026-07-20-9949e9fdf" ./run_benchmark.py
```

::: {#aac8adf4 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="`run_benchmark.py`, the script used to benchmark both versions of `gix blame`"}
#!/usr/bin/env python
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.13"
# ///

import os

def run(path, i):
    os.system(
        f'hyperfine --parameter-list command "$BASELINE_EXECUTABLE","$COMPARISON_EXECUTABLE" --parameter-list path {path} "{{command}} blame {{path}}" --command-name baseline --command-name comparison --export-json benchmark-{i}.json'
    )

for i, path in enumerate(
    [
        "CHANGELOG.md",
        "STABILITY.md",
        "README.md",
        "Cargo.toml",
        "gix-blame/src/file/function.rs",
        "gix-path/src/env/mod.rs",
        "gix-index/tests/index/file/write.rs",
        "gix-object/src/lib.rs",
        "gix-odb/src/store_impls/loose/write.rs",
    ]
):
    run(path, i + 1)
```
:::


This will create a couple of Markdown files, `benchmark-1.json` through
`benchmark-9.json`.

## Analyzing the data

Then, in order to work with these files, we’re going to use `numpy` and
`pandas` to load them into `data`.

::: {#283d4e5f .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="A few helper functions for loading the data"}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import matplotlib as mpl

import seaborn as sns

import json

def load_results(filename):
    with open(filename) as f:
        return json.load(f)["results"]

def extract_data_points(result):
    command = result["command"]
    path = result["parameters"]["path"]

    return {"command": command, "path": path, "time": result["times"]}
```
:::


::: {#a96c8d99 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
filenames = [f"benchmark-{i}.json" for i in range(1, 10)]
results = [load_results(filename) for filename in filenames]
results = [extract_data_points(result) for result in np.concatenate(results)]

data = pd.concat(
    [pd.DataFrame(result) for result in results],
    ignore_index=True,
)
```
:::


And finally, we’re going to create 2 plots that will give us an idea of how
both versions of `gix blame` compare with respect to performance. Looking in
particular at the boxplot, it seems that performance slightly regressed between
March and July. I don’t know yet whether this is due to a particular change,
and the effect is really small, so I’m not sure yet whether I’m going to
investigate this in depth.

## Creating a boxplot

::: {#99c2f7fc .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"}
FIGURE_WIDTH = 8
FIGURE_ASPECT = 1.6

sns.set_theme(
    palette="Paired",
    rc={"figure.figsize": (FIGURE_WIDTH, FIGURE_WIDTH / FIGURE_ASPECT)},
)
```
:::


::: {#022c699d .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
boxplot = sns.boxplot(x="time", y="path", hue="command", data=data)
sns.despine(offset=10, trim=True)
mpl.pyplot.tight_layout()
mpl.pyplot.show()

## Creating a stripplot

::: {#6c3711cc .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
mpl.pyplot.figure(figsize=(FIGURE_WIDTH * 0.75, FIGURE_WIDTH / FIGURE_ASPECT))

    x="time",
    y="path",
    hue="command",
    dodge=True,
    size=2.5,
    jitter=0.2,
    legend=False,
    data=data,
)
